newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-SHOW GOES ON AT AINTREE.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-SHOW GOES ON AT AINTREE.

text.p: Just when Aintree had begun to put the 1993 Grand National void race fiasco behind it, two cheap phone calls brought all the nightmares back.
How easy it was to bring a great event to its knees. How easy to spoil the party.
Last Friday Ian Latimer, police commander at Aintree, said "We have not had any specific threats from any organisations and we have a range of contingency plans to deal with any eventuality."

On Saturday those plans were there for all to see -- and the consequences to be endured. Around 70,000 people were evacuated, the race was called off and about 40,000 were left stranded with cars and coaches trapped overnight in one of the biggest security alerts ever seen in Britain.

After 14-1 chance Lord Gyllene had restored some semblance of normality on Monday, winning the re-scheduled race, the 150th, by 25 lengths, Latimer said "I feel a lot better now than I did at 2.50 on Saturday afternoon."
He described the last few days as "a highly sucessful policing operation." Praising the public and Aintree staff, he said: "We imposed quite severe limitations on them and they co-operated fully."
But he acknowledged: "There are many lessons that will be learned about the evacuation on Saturday and from the policing operation today."
Bloody but unbowed, the show had -- and has -- to go on.
That was the message from trainers, owners, officials and others and one heavily underscored by Prime Minister John Major who broke off from his electioneering to fly in by helicopter in on Monday.
The Queen's daughter Princess Anne, who had been there on Saturday, returned again on Monday to underline the point.
About 20,000 people, twice as many as expected, turned up to make their statement, although free admission clearly helped the attendance.
The race itself provided its usual spectacle with Lord Gyllene becoming the first horse for nearly 80 years to successfully make all the running.
It was an excellent performance and one which marked the swansong of Britain's "Voice of racing" Peter O'Sullevan, now 79 and making his 50th and final commentary on the race.
Ironically winning jockey Tony Dobbin is a Northern Irishman. Wisely, he declined to make any political comment, content rather to savour the greatest day of his life.

Charlie Brooks, trainer of runner-up Suny Bay and a man who once famously climbed a tree in protest at a proposed bypass, summed it up for many when he told reporters: "There is a sense of pride in racing today -- and we live to fight another day."
Unhappily, two horses will be fighting no more, the race claiming the lives of Smith's Band and Straight Talk.

The former was trained by Jenny Pitman who over the last few years has become part of Aintree folklore. She had been in tears over Saturday's events and was among the first to insist: "The race cannot not go on".
It went on and she lost one of her much loved horses - a truly bitter irony to round off a truly extraordinary three days.
